title: Section 142 — Wrongfully concealing or keeping in confinement, kidnapped or abducted person

content.overview: BNS s. 142 — Wrongfully concealing or keeping in confinement, kidnapped or abducted person.
content.study:
Introduction and meaning
Wrongfully concealing or keeping in confinement, kidnapped or abducted person. BNS restatement of IPC 368. Elements are substantially the same; cite the BNS number for offences on or after 1 July 2024. BNS restatement of IPC 368. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.
In student language: BNS s. 142 is the rule on “Wrongfully concealing or keeping in confinement, kidnapped or abducted person”. The section provides that whoever, knowing that any person has been kidnapped or has been abducted, wrongfully conceals or confines such person, shall be punished in the same manner as if he had kidnapped or abducted such person with the same intention or knowledge, or for the same purpose as that with or for which he conceals or detains such person in confinement. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 142 exists so that “Wrongfully concealing or keeping in confinement, kidnapped or abducted person” has a closed legal test in Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.

learningObjectives: Master the harbouring and confinement of kidnapped or abducted persons under BNS s. 142.
Analyze the scienter requirement: knowledge that the person has been kidnapped or abducted.
Understand the vicarious sentencing formula: punished in the same manner as if the accused had kidnapped or abducted the person.
Appreciate the consolidation of old IPC s. 368.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 142 provides that whoever, knowing that any person has been kidnapped or has been abducted, wrongfully conceals or confines such person, shall be punished in the same manner as if he had kidnapped or abducted such person with the same intention or knowledge, or for the same purpose as that with or for which he conceals or detains such person in confinement.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Eliminates safe harbors for kidnapping syndicates by holding custodians and guards who conceal kidnapped victims vicariously liable to the exact same punishment as the primary kidnappers.
statutoryFramework: Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body, BNS s. 142 (corresponding to IPC s. 368).
Scienter: Knowledge that the person has been kidnapped or abducted.
Actus reus: Wrongfully concealing or keeping the victim in confinement.
Sentencing formula: Punished in the exact same manner as if the accused had kidnapped or abducted the person with that intention or purpose.
essentialIngredients: A person was kidnapped or abducted.
The accused knew that the person had been kidnapped or abducted.
The accused wrongfully concealed or confined the person.
The accused acted with an unlawful intention or purpose.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 142 carries forward IPC 368. It targets safehouse keepers, caretakers, and conspirators who do not participate in the initial street abduction, but take custody of the kidnapped victim to hide them from police or families. The essential mens rea is knowledge: the accused must know that the person in their custody has been kidnapped or abducted. Once that knowledge is established, the act of concealing or confining the victim attracts the exact same punishment as if the accused had performed the kidnapping themselves. For instance, if a person conceals a victim knowing they were abducted for ransom under Section 140(2), the concealer faces capital punishment or life imprisonment under Section 142.
examples: Teaching example (Guarding a kidnap victim): A farm owner permits a gang to keep a kidnapped child inside his locked barn for a share of the ransom money, knowing the child was abducted. Under s. 142, the farm owner is punished exactly as a kidnapper for ransom under s. 140(2) (death or life imprisonment).

Teaching example (Lack of knowledge): A homeowner rents a room to a tenant who secretly holds a kidnapped minor inside; the homeowner has no knowledge or suspicion of the kidnapping. Section 142 does not apply due to absence of scienter.
distinctions: Section 142 vs Section 127 (Wrongful Confinement): Section 127 applies to general confinement (up to 1-3 years); Section 142 applies when the confined person is known to be kidnapped, elevating sentences to up to life or death.
Section 142 vs Harboring an Offender: Harboring an offender shelters the criminal; Section 142 shelters the victim of the kidnapping.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether an accused who agreed to hide a kidnapped businessman in his basement for five days while negotiations for a ₹10 crore ransom proceeded can argue he was merely a landlord.
Rule: Concealing a person known to be kidnapped for ransom attracts the full penalty of kidnapping for ransom under BNS s. 142.
Application: The accused knew the victim was an abducted hostage held for ransom and actively concealed him.
Conclusion: The accused is guilty under BNS s. 142 and liable to capital punishment or life imprisonment.

keyTakeaways: Penalizes wrongfully concealing or confining a person known to be kidnapped or abducted.
Requires actual knowledge of the prior kidnapping or abduction.
Punished in the exact same manner as the primary kidnapping offence.
Prevents safehouse operators and caretakers from escaping major felony penalties.
